sections.COMMENTS:
This composite source straddles the Maiella Massif, in the south-eastern side of the central Apennines. It approximately coincides with the mid-crustal portion of a large, low-angle thrust fault which dips SW-ward. This source may represent the southward extents of the deep seismogenic compression belt of the Marche pede-Apennines. It is interesting to notice that it is very close, and marginally overlaps with the broad seismogenic extensional belt that predominates along the axis of the central Apennine mountain chain.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Guidoboni and Ferrari, 2004; ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a concentration of damaging earthquakes in the area. In particular, this region at-large has been affected by the: 101 A.D. (Me 6.2) San Valentino in Abruzzo, the 1209 (Me 6.0) Appennino Abruzzese, the 30 December 1456 northern sub-event (Mw 6.0) Molise, the 3 November 1706 (Mw 6.8) Maiella, the 10 June 1841 (Me 5.0) Valle dell'Aventino, the 10 September 1881 (Mw 5.4) Chietino, the 12 February 1882 (Mw 5.3) Chietino, and the 26 September 1933 (Mw 5.9) Maiella earthquakes.
There has been an increasing interest concerning the hints of tectonic activity in the eastern piedmont of south-eastern Abruzzo (Galadini et al., 2006; Fracassi and Valensise, 2007; De Nardis, 2008), posing a number of seismotectonic issues, none of them easy to solve. As a matter of fact, the region has been hit by at least one major earthquake such at the 1706 one, for which no solid solution had been proposed in the literature. The 1933 event, just east of the 1706 epicenter and conceivably with something in common with the former, did not help to elucidate the tectonic mechanism governing this sector. Just to complicate matters, both historical and instrumental catalogs show a puzzling "seismic silence" precisely in the coastal region (historically known as "Abruzzo Citeriore", following a Middle Ages nomenclature), but for very few Mw ca. 4 events.
There are numerous interpretations concerning the tectonic arrangement and structural style of the Mio-Pliocene to early Pleistocene compressional system east of the extensional axis in this sector of the Italian peninsula. Seismic reflection data, even those aimed at deep crustal studies (CROP 11; for a summary see: Patacca and Scandone, 2008), have imaged only partially the thrust system that has been known for some time thanks to industrial exploration.
Some authors have hypothesized a Late Pleistocene-Holocene compressional activity associated with the Abruzzi Coastal structure (de Nardis et al., 2007; de Nardis et al., 2008; Pomposo and Pizzi, 2009) and a potential seismogenic source has been presented by Lavecchia and de Nardis (2009). This Composite Source synthesizes their model. These authors have focused on the seismogenic role of the large reverse fault system, which they have named Abruzzo Citeriore Basal Thrust (ACBT), that underpins the coastal structures and deepens SW-ward, reaching mid-crustal depths (10-15 km) beneath the Maiella Massif. Through the integrated interpretation of structural data and intensity-data search-grid inversion results, they have isolated patches of the ACBT that, in their view, are the best candidates as individual seismogenic sources for the the 1706, 1933 and 1881 events.
Conversely, Patacca and Scandone (2008) consider the thrusting activity in the eastern Abruzzo area sealed since Late Pleistocene times, and associate the Casoli-Bomba anticline with a large backthrust, which offsets the Maiella anticline basal thrust and deepens NE-ward within the Adriatic foreland. In their interpretation, the Maiella Basal Thrust has been top-cut by a major backthrust, rooted just above the crystalline basement (15-20 km).
Also by analogy with the compressional seismotectonic setting of the pede-Apennine and coastal areas of the Marche region (Lavecchia et al., 2007), we interpret the ACBT to be the fault system that has emplaced the Casoli-Bomba structural high and that roots at ca. 18 km below the eastern flank of the Maiella massif. We maintain that a major segment of the ACBT is the causative source of the 3 November 1706 (Mw 6.8) earthquake; we then regard a further, smaller and slightly shallower segment as the causative source of then 23 September 1933 (Mw 6.0) event. Finally, in our interpretation, we contend that an upper crust segment of the ACBT (up-dip) is the causative source of the 1881 earthquake. Therefore, we interpret the latter as a portion of the same large thrust system.
The strike of the composite source was based on the interpretation of structural data and regional sections by Lavecchia and de Nardis (2009), as well as the dip and the rake, which is indicative of pure reverse faulting. The minimum and maximum depth were based on the geological interpretation by Lavecchia and de Nardis (2009). Slip rate was inferred from geological observations in adjacent structures, that share the same tectonic environment with this Source.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) What is the interaction (if any) of the ACBT with the deep-seated E-W, right-lateral strike-slip crustal faults that dissect the Apulian foreland, like the "Tremiti Lithospheric Tear" defined in Scrocca (2007) and/or the E-W buried strike slip faults proposed by Fracassi and Valensise (2007) that would lie beneath the ACBT to the north?
2) What is the structural arrangement of the ACBT at depth? Could it be an outer splay of the Maiella Basal Thrust? Is it still active?
3) Regardless of its rooting, if the ACBT is active and capable of accumulating (and releasing) seismic energy, what can we say about the Maiella Basal Thrust? The compressional activity ended in early Pliocene times, but might it now be inverted and active as a basal extensional detachment of the SW-dipping Morrone-Porrara normal faults (Lavecchia et al., 2010)? In such a case, could it be the causative source of the 3 November 1706 (Mw 6.8) Maiella earthquake, or even of the 1933 one?
